source.title: Memorization-Dilation: Modeling Neural Collapse Under Label Noise
source.authors: D. Nguyen; R. Levie; Julian Lienen; Gitta Kutyniok; E. Hüllermeier

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how memorization of noisy labels relates to test-feature collapse and test accuracy, and compares losses. Those findings concern generalization but do not test the specific behaviors in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports label-noise experiments and loss comparisons. Its neural-collapse and memorization measurements are its own results; cited results from prior work are excluded. Table 2 reports test accuracies for CE and LS, but these do not test any listed version.
record.test_reason: The study tests a memorization–dilation model and compares classification losses, but its own results do not test V1–V8. Partial label corruption and a feature-distance memorization metric do not establish V1's random-label fitting comparison or V8's example-removal effect.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors characterize neural collapse with positive features, then propose a memorization–dilation model supported by experiments. Under the binary, low-noise model assumptions, they prove that LS produces less memorization and normalized dilation than CE, offering one explanation for improved generalization. Empirical improvements are not universal, particularly without label noise; the model also omits memorization of clean examples.
record.recipe_differences: Studies noisy-label memorization, neural-collapse dilation, and label-loss comparisons rather than the interventions and measurements in V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, label-noise degree, loss, feature dimension, and architecture are varied across experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: At lower memorization levels, square-root test NC1 is approximately linear in the study's feature-distance memorization metric. CE and LS approximately share this curve; other losses can differ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested label-noise settings, feature-space memorization tracks degradation of test-feature collapse.

fits_no_version.finding: At η = 0.3, LS has higher mean test accuracy than CE for all eight dataset–architecture combinations. The reported uncertainties do not establish significance for every comparison. Noiseless results include exceptions to the authors' broad improvement statement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label smoothing can improve test accuracy relative to cross-entropy under partial training-label corruption.

record.problems: The main dilation and test-accuracy trends are presented in figures without tabulated values in the supplied text. The large-scale experiment reports averages and standard deviations over 3 seeds. The model's theoretical analysis is limited to two classes, and the authors note that their model omits memorization of clean examples.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 also reports η=0, 0.1, and 0.2 for each of four datasets and two architectures. Those 24 additional CE-versus-LS comparisons are omitted to stay within the row limit while retaining the η=0.3 comparisons across every dataset and architecture. Figures 1–9 report additional test-collapse and test-accuracy results, but their plotted values are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text; the paper's prose describes the aggregate trends.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fully randomized labels, chance held-out accuracy under random labels, and above-chance natural-label accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error; varying feature dimension and measuring dilation does not establish this.
Controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and their dependence on dataset size, dropout strength, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Influence-based identification of memorized examples followed by removal and retraining versus equal-sized random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The extraction's T2 designation conflicts with its correct observation that none of V1–V8 is tested. The cited discussion of memorization of clean examples does not itself test V8. No additional version-relevant results require missing rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting fixed random labels with generalization on natural labels under the same recipe.
Varies feature dimension in some experiments, but does not sweep network width across the zero-training-error threshold.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected architectures on the claimed local-connectivity question.
Uses SGD; does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD.
Uses fixed batch size 512; does not compare batch sizes or large-batch training.
Compares label smoothing with other losses, not dropout.
Measures neural-collapse dilation and memorization, not magnitude-aware sharpness or the listed norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.
